title: Quantum orientation, Noether structure, composition of systems and operations
abstract: In this paper we argue that, in addition to the statistical structure of quantum theory, another structure, referred to here as the ``Noether structure," is necessary to describe the composition of systems and to define completely positive operations. A Noether structure reflects the dual role of Hermitian operators as observables on the one hand and as generators of symmetry transformations on the other. This idea has been expressed in a similar form in the works of Alfsen and Shultz, who investigated the conditions under which the Jordan product can be extended to an associative product of operator algebras. Our investigations into the Noether structure and the composition of systems are limited to the finite-dimensional case and establish a connection to completely positive operations. In the case of pure operations, the latter can be characterized as orientation-preserving maps.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates the fundamental axioms governing quantum theory, arguing that a 'Noether structure' is necessary alongside statistical rules to properly describe composite systems. Using advanced mathematics involving principal bundles and geometric invariants, the authors prove that the composition of subsystems is not uniquely determined by standard axioms alone. The work establishes deep mathematical constraints on the very foundations of quantum mechanics.
main_problem: The paper argues that quantum theory requires a structure beyond mere statistical description—the 'Noether structure'—to correctly model system composition and define completely positive operations.
main_result: The statistical structure alone is insufficient to uniquely determine the composition of composite quantum systems, necessitating the inclusion of this additional Noether structure or 'quantum orientation'.
method: The analysis uses axiomatic comparisons between standard quantum probability structures ($\langle K, L, \mu angle$) and requirements for tensor product decomposition, supplemented by advanced geometric tools involving principal bundles and $Z_2$-bundles.
model_or_system: The focus is on the foundational axioms of Quantum Theory (QT) applied to finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces ($H$), considering the composition of two subsystems ($\mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \mathcal{H}_2$).
key_observables: Statistical structure $\langle K, L, \mu angle$, observables, and the resulting 'quantum orientation' defined geometrically.
important_parameters: Finite dimensionality ($N$), the specific choice of product structures ($\mu_{12} = \mu_1 \mu_2$), and geometric invariants related to $O(3)$ bundles.
main_assumptions: The analysis is strictly limited to the finite-dimensional case, and certain proofs rely on assumptions about the rank or number of terms in quantum operations ($n>1$).

It then employs advanced differential geometry (principal bundles, $Z_2$-bundles) to define necessary global structures (Chunk 3), concluding with a detailed analysis of pure quantum operations using rank arguments (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: This work tackles the foundational structure of quantum mechanics itself, providing deep mathematical constraints on how physical processes like composition and evolution must be mathematically formulated beyond standard state/effect descriptions.
